title: A Saturday at the market
paragraphs: Every Saturday, Efua goes to the big market in the city centre. She usually leaves home at seven o'clock, before the streets get busy. She takes a shared taxi because it is cheaper than a private one.

At the market, she buys vegetables, fish and rice for the whole week. She always visits the same seller, Mrs Agbo, because her tomatoes are fresh and her prices are fair. They often chat about their families.

This Saturday is different. Efua is not shopping for food. She is looking for a present for her brother, who is graduating next week. After an hour, she finds a beautiful leather bag. It is expensive, but she decides to buy it. "He will use it every day at his new job," she thinks.

shared.def: used by several people at the same time

chat.def: to talk in a friendly, informal way

summary: Efua shops at the market every Saturday, always from the same seller. This week she buys a leather bag as a graduation present for her brother.

title: How mobile money changed daily life
paragraphs: Twenty years ago, sending money to a relative in another town was slow and risky. People often gave cash to a bus driver or travelled for hours to deliver it themselves. Today, in many West African countries, a few taps on a basic phone are enough.

Mobile money services allow users to store money in an account linked to their phone number. They can transfer it, pay bills or buy airtime without a bank account. This has been especially important for people in rural areas, where banks are rare and often far away.

Researchers have found that families who use mobile money are better able to deal with emergencies, such as an illness or a poor harvest, because relatives can send help quickly. Small traders also benefit: they can receive payments from customers they have never met.

However, the system is not perfect. Transaction fees can be high for small amounts, and fraud — for example, fake messages asking users to send money back — remains a problem. Experts argue that better digital education is as important as new technology.

relative.fr: un proche, membre de la famille

airtime.def: phone credit for calls and data

emergencies.def: sudden dangerous situations needing quick action

harvest.def: the crops collected in a season

traders.def: people who buy and sell goods

summary: Mobile money lets people transfer and store money with a phone, which helps rural families, emergencies and small traders. Problems remain: high fees for small amounts and fraud, so digital education is needed.

title: Why sleep helps you learn
paragraphs: Many students believe that staying up late is the best way to prepare for an exam. Scientific studies suggest the opposite: sleep plays an essential role in learning.

During the day, the brain collects new information. At night, especially during deep sleep, it reorganises this information and transfers important memories to long-term storage. In one well-known type of experiment, people who slept after learning a list of words remembered more of them the next day than people who stayed awake.
Sleep also affects attention. After a short night, it is harder to concentrate, and we make more mistakes. This is why a tired student may read the same page several times without understanding it.
For language learners, the message is clear: regular short study sessions followed by a good night's sleep are more effective than one long session the night before a test.

storage.def: a place where things are kept

summary: Sleep helps learning because the brain reorganises and stores memories at night and attention is better after rest. Short regular sessions plus sleep beat one long late-night session.
